What about the 1,473 marine species figure?

A 2024 OBIS/UNESCO analysis counted 1,473 marine species in three IUCN risk groups together: Vulnerable, Endangered and Critically Endangered. “Endangered” is just one of those groups. Counts change when assessments change.

SeaDex is a separate guide, not the complete IUCN Red List. It combines 107 help profiles with 1,353 extra species records from OBIS, after matching older and newer animal names to avoid repeats. Those OBIS labels may be older than the latest IUCN ratings.

Read the 2024 OBIS report

Extra records have source links and general tips. Their full threat lists have not been checked.

Sources, dates and what this guide covers

The 107 help profiles include the 105 entries in NOAA’s threatened-and-endangered directory, plus whale shark and African penguin profiles. Some cover protected groups or subspecies. Two river-only dolphins are labeled.

The 1,353 extra records come from the OBIS Red List checklist, filtered to animals marked as marine and listed there as Vulnerable, Endangered or Critically Endangered. Names were matched with WoRMS to avoid adding the same animal under an older name. English names are shown where the source provides them. Otherwise, use the science name.

Copied November 21, 2026. OBIS does not supply an assessment date in this response and can lag behind IUCN updates. Extra records do not have checked species-specific threat lists. Their tips are for the animal group. Their videos are clearly labeled related footage.

U.S. legal protection and worldwide extinction risk are different. Neither the SeaDex total nor the 2024 figure is a complete, live count of all endangered marine animals.

OBIS (2026). Ocean Biodiversity Information System. Intergovernmental Oceanographic Commission of UNESCO. Names: WoRMS Editorial Board (2026), World Register of Marine Species. Risk categories supplied by OBIS from IUCN. Accessed November 21, 2026.

Learn more about the problems and fixes
The problem, in a few words

Ocean animals need safer homes.

Plastic, harmful fishing and warmer seas put ocean animals in danger. Protecting their homes and changing a few habits can help.

Power use and ocean life

How energy affects animals.

The way we make power can affect both the sea and the rivers that lead to it.

Fuel, heat and seawater

Burning coal, oil or gas to make electricity releases gases that trap heat and warm the ocean. The sea also takes in some carbon dioxide, making the water more acidic. That makes it harder for corals and some shellfish to build their hard outer parts.

What helps: waste less power and support cleaner energy.

Water power and blocked fish

Hydro dams make electricity from moving water. But they can block fish, such as salmon, travelling between rivers and the sea. Dams can change water flow, and their spinning machines can hurt fish.

What helps: safe routes around dams, screens to keep fish away from machines, and river flows that support fish. The right fix depends on the river and the fish.

Learn more: NOAA: carbon dioxide and seawater · NOAA: helping fish pass dams

Ocean terms explained

Endangered means a species faces a very high risk of extinction in the wild. Bycatch means animals caught accidentally while fishing for something else. Conservation means keeping wild animals and their homes safe.

How you can help

Start at any age: reuse a bottle, share what you learned, or join a supervised cleanup. Families and communities can also support habitat protection and policies that make fishing safer.

About conservation status

An animal may be doing well worldwide but still be in danger in some places. Green turtles moved to Least Concern worldwide in 2025. They still need protection. The checklist tracks your actions, not the number of animals saved.
